text: Welcome! On this very first slide you can see the whole market puzzle laid out.
I spot a colourful list: demand, revenue, elasticity, supply… looks busy!
Exactly. Before we solve anything, let's gather the gifts the examiner already handed us—our “givens.”
I like free gifts. First one: the demand curve sitting in the top-left corner.
Yes—notice it links quantity q to price p through that four plus p squared denominator.
Got it. Next, the bullet that says revenue equals p times q.
Perfect. Revenue will let us talk about money flows later.
There’s also a price jump from one to one point one. Seems tiny but important.
Right—think of it as a gentle tap on the price knob. We’ll use differentials to predict the ripple in revenue.
I also read “inverse supply equals alpha q plus beta.” Two mysterious symbols to uncover!
They won’t stay mysterious for long. The equilibrium point—two comma four—gives us one equation, while the producer surplus of two gives us another.
So two unknowns, two equations—straight-line algebra territory.
Exactly. Tool-wise, our backpack needs differentiation, elasticity formula, linear approximation, and a pinch of definite integration for surplus.
All stuff from first-year calculus and intro micro-economics. Phew, within reach.
Great job summarising. Any anxieties before we dive?
Just eager to see how elasticity can never break the ceiling of two. Sounds like a magic trick.
Then let’s roll up our sleeves. On the next slide we’ll take the demand curve apart with the chain rule. Ready?
Ready and curious!
Now, eyes on the demand expression highlighted in blue.
I see the price buried inside that four plus p squared denominator.
Question: how would you start finding dq divided by dp?
Rewrite q as ten times that denominator to the power negative one, then apply the chain rule.
Superb. Give it a shot—what’s the derivative sign wise?
The negative pops out, and I get something like minus twenty p over the denominator squared.
Exactly—great algebraic footwork.
Next comes elasticity. Formula says E equals negative dq divided by dp times p divided by q.
Correct. Plug in your derivative and the original q. Notice one power of the denominator cancels—like peeling an onion layer.
Oh, neat! The dust settles to two p squared over four plus p squared.
Spot on. That’s our clean elasticity function.
Feels satisfying to see the clutter disappear.
And that cancellation trick will keep life simple in the following slide.
So we’re armed with E of p. What’s next?
We’ll test whether this expression can ever climb beyond two. Onward!
Look at the tidy formula we boxed in the top-right: two p squared divided by four plus p squared.
The numerator looks like a little sibling to the denominator—same p squared but without the four.
Brilliant observation. For any non-negative p, is p squared smaller than four plus p squared?
Absolutely—because you’re adding four in the denominator.
Therefore, the fraction p squared over four plus p squared is always less than one, yet never negative.
Multiply by two and I see elasticity lives between zero and two.
Exactly—so our demand never reaches unit trouble beyond two.
Meaning the curve is relatively inelastic compared with, say, luxury-goods examples.
That’s a nice economic interpretation.
Wow, the “never exceed two” claim was just a direct comparison, no extra calculus!
Sometimes math rewards keen eyesight over brute force. Great job.
Feeling confident. Let’s put this elasticity badge in our pocket.
Next stop: building the revenue mountain and finding its peak.
Shift your gaze to the green box labelled revenue R of p.
It’s ten p divided by four plus p squared—smooth.
We need the slope, dR divided by dp. Think quotient rule or product rule-with-negative-power—dealer’s choice.
I’ll go negative-power again: derivative of p is one, derivative of the denominator piece adds the minus sign…*
Keep going.
I end up with ten over four plus p squared minus twenty p squared over the denominator squared.
Excellent. Combine them under a common denominator.
Factor ten and I get ten times four minus p squared all over the denominator squared.
Perfect. Now, what sign does four minus p squared take?
Positive when p is less than two, zero at p equals two, negative after two.
Translate that into revenue talk.
Revenue climbs while price is below two and tumbles once price climbs above two.
Beautiful economic story: there’s a sweet-spot price of two where revenue tops out.
Like hiking a hill—up until the summit at two, then down the other side.
Exactly. Summit reached. Ready for a small price step analysis?
Bring on the tiny hike from one to one point one!
Zoom into the red rectangle—linear approximation toolbox.
The plan: delta R is roughly derivative at one times delta p.
Spot on. What’s delta p here?
One tenth—zero point one.
Earlier we had the derivative formula: ten times four minus p squared over the denominator squared. Plug p equals one.
Numerator gives thirty, denominator becomes twenty-five, so derivative is one point two.
Nice arithmetic. Multiply by delta p.
One point two times zero point one equals zero point one two.
Meaning revenue should rise by about twelve pence per unit timeframe.
So a gentle uphill nudge, matching the earlier “revenue increasing for p less than two” insight.
Exactly—consistency check passed.
Linear approximation really is a handy pocket lens.
And you wielded it well. Final leg: cracking the supply curve parameters.
Front and centre is the orange supply line: p superscript S equals alpha q plus beta.
We know the market rests at two units, four currency units price. Plugging those should tie alpha and beta together.
Right—substituting gives our first equation: two alpha plus beta equals four.
Noted. Now for the producer surplus clue.
Surplus is the triangular-looking area between the supply curve and the horizontal price at four, from zero to two units.
So integrate four minus the supply price with respect to q over zero to two.
Exactly. Performing that integration leaves a tidy expression: two times four minus beta minus two alpha.
Setting that equal to two gives four minus beta minus alpha equals one.
Great. Line them up: Equation one—two alpha plus beta equals four. Equation two—alpha plus beta equals three.
Subtract to solve: alpha equals one.
Substitute back and beta becomes two.
Therefore the inverse supply curve is p superscript S equals q plus two.
Well done! You transformed abstract symbols into a concrete line.
Feels like finishing a puzzle—every piece snug.
Celebrate this victory. We’ve threaded calculus, algebra, and economics into one coherent story.
Thanks for the guidance. Time to share this newfound knowledge with my study group!
